source_text: Videamus nune breviter quid etiam de repromissionibus sentiendum sit. Certum est quia nullum animal omnimodis otiosum atque immobile esse potest, sed omni genere moveri et agere semper et velle aliquid gestit; et hanc inesse naturam omnibus animantibus manifestum puto. Multo ergo magis rationabile animal, id est hominis naturam necesse est semper aliquid movere vel agere. Et si quidem immemor sui sit eb quid se deceat ignoret, circa usus corporales omnis sua movetur intentio et per omnes motus suos erga voluptates ac libidines corporis oecupatur; si vero talis sit, qui in commune aliquid curare vel providere studeat, aut rei publicae consulens aut magistratibus parens aut quidquid illud est, quod in commune certe prodesse videatur, exercet. Jam vero si qui talis sit, ut aliquid melius quam haee, quae corporea videntur, intellegat et sapientiae ac scientiae operam navet, sine dubio erga huiuscemodi studia omnem sui declinabit industriam, quo possit inquisita veritate rerum causas rationemque cognoscere. Nicut ergo in hae vita alius quidem summum bonum corporis iudicat voluptatem, alius vero in commune consulere, alius studus et intellegentiae operam dare: ita requirimus in illa “vitae quae vera est, quae “abscondita essedicitur -cum Christo in deo’, id est in illa aeterna vita, si aliqui talis erii nobis vivendi ordo vel status.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see now briefly what is to be thought also about the promises. It is certain that no animal at all can be idle and immobile, but it is moved and acts always and desires something; and I think it is manifest that this nature is in all living things. Much more therefore the rational animal, that is the nature of man, it is necessary always to move or do something. And if indeed he is forgetful of himself and ignores what is fitting for him, his whole intention is moved around bodily uses and through all his movements he is occupied with the pleasures and desires of the body; if however he is such that he strives to care for or provide for something in common, either consulting for the state or obeying magistrates or whatever that is which certainly seems to be of use in common, he exercises. Now indeed if someone is such that he understands something better than these bodily things and devotes himself to wisdom and knowledge, without doubt he will direct all his industry towards such studies, so that he may know the causes and reason of things investigated. Just as therefore in this life one judges the greatest good of the body to be pleasure, another to consult for the common good, another to devote himself to studies and intelligence: so we require in that life which is true, which is called hidden, with Christ in God, that is in that eternal life, if such a one will be for us the order or status of living.

choices.why: comparing bodily things to intellectual pursuits
describing the location of eternal life

pass_b_english: Let's consider briefly what we should think about the promises. It's certain that no animal can be completely idle and immobile, but instead is always moving and acting, and desires something - and it's clear that this nature is present in all living things. So, it's even more necessary for the rational animal, that is, human nature, to always be doing something. If someone is forgetful of themselves and doesn't know what's fitting for them, their whole intention is focused on physical needs and they're occupied with bodily pleasures and desires through all their actions. On the other hand, if someone strives to care for or provide for something that benefits everyone, whether by consulting for the state, obeying authorities, or doing something else that seems to be of common benefit, they exercise this inclination. Furthermore, if someone understands that there's something more important than physical things and devotes themselves to wisdom and knowledge, they will undoubtedly direct all their effort towards these studies, so that they may understand the causes and reasons behind things. Just as some people in this life consider the greatest good to be bodily pleasure, others think it's consulting for the common good, and others believe it's pursuing studies and intelligence, we require a similar approach in the true life, which is called hidden, with Christ in God - that is, in eternal life, if such a way of living will be our standard.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A is a faithful literal translation, and Pass B is a fluent rendering that preserves all nuances of agency and modality. The phrase 'cum Christo in deo' is correctly rendered in both as 'with Christ in God'.
